Remote-first data, software & AI consultancy

## Senior engineers who work in your timezone, without the consultancy overhead.

MV.tech builds data pipelines, business software, automation and AI systems for companies worldwide. You work directly with the specialists doing the engineering, we plan our hours around yours, and you never pay for offices, account layers or a bench.

What we do

### Six ways to bring senior engineering into your business.

01 / Data

#### Data engineering consulting

ETL and ELT pipelines, BigQuery, Snowflake and Redshift warehouses, migrations off legacy reporting, semantic models and data quality checks. Python and SQL done properly.

02 / Software

#### Custom software development

Business web applications, client portals, dashboards and internal tools, with the interface, integrations and data backend designed together.

03 / AI

#### AI automation, RAG & MCP development

Knowledge assistants grounded in your documents, Model Context Protocol servers that expose approved tools, and LLM features integrated into existing products.

04 / Automation

#### Workflow automation & API integration

Connect the systems your team moves data between by hand. Scheduled jobs, webhooks, validation and monitoring with clear ownership.

05 / Team

#### IT staff augmentation

Add a senior remote data, software, cloud or AI consultant to your existing team, with capacity, responsibilities and overlap hours agreed up front.

06 / Hiring

#### Technology recruitment

Hire permanent AI, data, software and cloud professionals into your own organisation, with an engineer shaping the brief and assessing fit.

How remote works with us

### Based in India. Working in your hours.

India Standard Time sits between the Asia-Pacific and American working days, which lets a team in Ahmedabad share a real working window with almost any client. Before an engagement starts we agree when we overlap, how decisions get recorded and how you see progress between calls.

- Agreed overlap, not vague availability — A recurring window in your timezone for standups, reviews and releases. US Eastern mornings, UK and European afternoons, Gulf and APAC business hours are all routine.
- Written progress you can forward — Decisions, demos and open questions are documented in your tools, so your stakeholders stay informed without another meeting.
- The people you meet do the work — No account managers or hand-offs to a junior bench. Scope, estimates and delivery come from the same senior engineers.
Engagement models

### Choose the working model that fits the work.

#### Scoped project

A defined outcome with milestones, acceptance criteria and handover. Best for a first data pipeline, an application, an automation or an AI assistant with a clear boundary.

#### Embedded consultant or team

Senior specialists working inside your team, in your tools and your hours, for an agreed capacity and duration. Best when you need depth and pace without a permanent hire.

#### Permanent recruitment

Hire into your own organisation with an engineering-led search: a precise brief, technical screening and a shortlist you can trust. Best when the role is long-term.

How MV.tech compares with the usual alternatives
| Consideration | MV.tech remote team | Large consultancy | Freelance marketplace |
| Who does the work | Senior specialists you speak with directly | Layered account, delivery and offshore teams | One individual; depth varies |
| Timezone overlap | Planned around your hours, any timezone | Usually local hours only | Depends on the individual |
| Overhead you pay for | Lean remote model, no office or account layers | Offices, account management, bench costs | Low, but no team behind the work |
| Continuity and cover | Team-backed, documented handover | Yes, at consultancy rates | Single point of failure |
| Pricing | Agreed per engagement against a written scope | Premium day rates and minimum commitments | Hourly, with scope drift risk |

Common questions

### What people ask before they book a call.

More detail is in the full FAQ and on how we work.

**What does MV.tech do?**
MV.tech is a remote-first consultancy that provides data engineering, custom software development, workflow automation, AI development (including RAG systems and MCP servers), IT staff augmentation and technology recruitment. We are based in Ahmedabad, India, and work with clients worldwide.

**How does timezone overlap work with a team in India?**
We agree a recurring collaboration window in your local time before the engagement begins, for example 9:00 am to 1:00 pm US Eastern, 9:00 am to 3:30 pm in the UK, or 12:30 pm to 6:00 pm in Sydney. Standups, reviews and releases happen inside that window; written updates and documented decisions cover the rest of the day.

**Why is MV.tech less expensive than a large consultancy?**
You pay for senior engineering time, not for offices, account management layers or idle bench capacity. Pricing is agreed per engagement against a written scope. We do not claim to be the cheapest option; we aim to be the best value for senior work with direct access to the people doing it.

**How does an engagement start?**
Book a 30-minute call or email a short brief. We clarify the goal, current systems and constraints, then propose a first milestone with deliverables, review points and the overlap hours. Work starts only after that scope is agreed in writing.

**Can MV.tech work inside our existing team and tools?**
Yes. Through IT staff augmentation our consultants join your team in your repositories, ticketing and communication tools, under the direction of your technical leads, with agreed capacity and responsibilities. We can also own a scoped project end to end.

**Is MV.tech the same company as MV Tech Solutions or MVTech?**
Yes. MV.tech is the official brand, and mvtech.solutions is the official website. MV Tech, MVTech, MV Tech Solutions and MV Tech Ahmedabad are common search variants of the same company.

Start a conversation

### Tell us what needs to work better.

Describe the goal, the systems involved and your preferred working hours. A 30-minute scoping call is enough to tell you whether we are the right fit and what a sensible first milestone looks like.

About MV.tech

## A remote-first team of senior engineering specialists.

MV.tech is a data engineering, software development and AI consultancy based in Ahmedabad, India. We build cloud warehouses and pipelines, the analytics and BI layers on top of them, business software and AI automation. We work with companies worldwide, plan our working hours around theirs, and keep the team deliberately small so clients always deal with the people doing the engineering.

Founder

### Led by an engineer, not an account manager.

### Meet Vaghasia — Founder & Lead Engineer

Meet is a senior data and AI engineer. His hands-on work covers Python and SQL pipelines into BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift and PostgreSQL, enterprise analytics migrations off legacy databases and manual reporting, dimensional and semantic models behind Power BI, Tableau, Looker Studio and Streamlit, and AI automation built with RAG, Model Context Protocol servers and custom AI connectors. He is Toptal-vetted (Top 3% of applicants) and holds Google Cloud and IBM credentials.

That experience runs from enterprise reporting estates and financial data platforms through to on-chain analytics, which is why MV.tech treats reconciliation, access control, documentation and handover as part of the build rather than a later phase. He founded the company to give clients direct access to senior engineering without the layers, bench costs and hand-offs of a large consultancy.

How we operate

### What "remote-first and lean" means in practice.

#### Senior people, end to end

The engineers who scope the work build it, review it and hand it over. There is no junior bench behind the proposal and no account manager between you and the team.

#### Your hours, agreed in advance

India Standard Time overlaps every major business region for part of the day. We fix a collaboration window in your local time and keep decisions written down between calls.

#### Overhead you do not pay for

No offices to fund, no sales layer, no idle capacity. Pricing is agreed per engagement against a written scope, so the cost reflects the work rather than the brand.

#### Scope before commitment

Every engagement starts with a first milestone, acceptance criteria and review points. You can judge the working relationship on something real before expanding it.

#### Careful with your data

Least-privilege access, separated environments and credentials handled the way you would expect from an engineering team that also runs production systems. See our delivery standards.

#### Honest about fit

If a problem does not need us, or needs something other than software, we say so on the first call. Long relationships come from useful advice, not from selling every project.

MV.tech is a compact company, but the experience behind it comes from enterprise, platform and product work: analytics modernisation programmes moving legacy reporting into a cloud warehouse, financial and operational data platforms where every figure has to reconcile, and AI automation connected to real business systems. # MV.tech Brand Kit: Logos, Colours, Fonts & Guidelines

URL: https://mvtech.solutions/brand/
Description: Download the MV.tech brand kit: vector logos, favicons, avatars, the colour palette as design tokens, Inter fonts, icons and the full brand guidelines.
Last modified: 2026-09-12

Brand assets

## The MV.tech brand kit, ready to use.

Everything you need to represent MV.tech correctly in an article, a partner deck, a directory listing or a co-branded page. Vector logo masters, favicons and avatars, the colour palette as design tokens, the Inter type family, the icon set and the full guidelines.

Download the brand kit ZIP · 15 MB Ask for print files

What is inside

### Eight folders, no guesswork.

#### Vector masters

The logo as true vector, SVG and PDF, in every variant: horizontal, primary and vertical lockups, the monogram and the wordmark, each in dark, light and single colour. Send these to printers and designers.

#### Ready-made exports

PNG at 512 and 1024 pixels for every variant, so you rarely need to open a vector editor.

#### Favicons and app icons

favicon.ico, an SVG favicon, Apple touch icon, Android and maskable icons, a Safari pinned-tab mark and a ready-made head snippet.

#### Social avatars

Circle-safe profile images sized for LinkedIn, X, Instagram, YouTube, WhatsApp and Google Business.

#### Colour and design tokens

The palette as JSON, CSS custom properties, SCSS, a Tailwind config, W3C design tokens, Adobe and GIMP swatches, and an Office theme.

#### Type

Inter for desktop and web with its open font licence, plus a type specimen and the rules for sizes, weights and letter-spacing.

#### Icon set

Brand icons in three colourways as SVG and PNG, with app-style tiles.

#### Guidelines

The full brand guidelines and a one-page quick reference covering logo use, clear space, minimum sizes, colour, accessibility and misuse.

Using the logo

### Five rules that cover almost every case.

- Use the vector masters.They are the source of truth. The PNGs are for everyday work.
- Match the logo to the background.Dark surfaces take the silver logo, white and pale surfaces the navy one.
- When you cannot control the background,use a file ending-on-inkor-on-white. Each carries its own background and clear space.
- Keep one dot of clear space.Nothing may enter the area around the logo equal to the teal dot's diameter.
- MV never appears twice.The monogram is the letters M and V, and its dot is the full stop, so a lockup pairs the mark withtechonly, never with the full wordmark. Never retype the wordmark in a font.
Do not stretch, rotate, recolour or add effects to the logo, and do not place it on a busy or low-contrast area. The guidelines in the download show the misuses in full.

Colour

### The palette, and where each colour is allowed.

| Name | Hex | Use |
| Ink | #05060B | Primary dark background |
| Navy | #071118 | Body text on light backgrounds, and the mark on white |
| Signal Teal | #10F5D0 | Accent and highlights on dark. Decorative only on white |
| System Cyan | #00BFCB | Gradient support and separators |
| Teal Ink | #007E7B | The only teal for links and small text on white |
| Silver | #F4F6F8 | Light surfaces and the mark on dark |
| Graphite | #405466 | Secondary text on light backgrounds |
Signal Teal and System Cyan do not meet accessibility contrast requirements for text on white, so on light backgrounds they are used for shapes and borders rather than words. Full contrast data ships with the download.

### Need the print files?

The download covers logos, colour, type, icons and the guidelines. Print-ready business cards with bleed and crop marks, letterhead, the company one-pager, Word and PowerPoint templates, email signatures and the complete social set are part of the full kit. Ask us and we will send them.

# Privacy, Security & Delivery Standards | MV.tech

URL: https://mvtech.solutions/compliance/
Description: How MV.tech handles client data, credentials and access: secure remote delivery, accessibility, website analytics and responsible use of automation and AI.
Last modified: 2026-09-11

Trust, security & compliance

## Professional delivery standards for responsible systems.

Practical security, careful data handling, transparent communication and clear project boundaries. This page explains how we work with your data and systems, and how this website itself handles visitor information.

Delivery standards

### What you can expect on every engagement.

#### Data privacy

Client data is handled only for agreed project purposes, with access limited to what delivery needs. We work in your environments where possible and do not retain client data after handover unless a support agreement requires it.

#### Secure delivery

Least-privilege access granted by you, separated development and production environments, secrets kept in your secret management, API security and access reviews during the engagement and at handover.

#### Accessibility

Web interfaces are planned with semantic structure, keyboard navigation, readable contrast and responsive layouts, following WCAG 2.1 AA as the working target unless a project specifies otherwise.

#### Clear terms

Scope, ownership, timelines, support and third-party responsibilities are documented before work begins. Mutual NDAs and your master services agreement are welcome.

This website

### Privacy notice for visitors.

- Information you send us
  Details submitted by email or through our scheduling link are used to respond to your enquiry, prepare proposals, deliver agreed services and maintain client communication. We do not sell or share enquiry data with third parties for marketing.
- Analytics
  This site uses Google Analytics 4 to understand aggregate traffic and improve the website. Analytics measures clicks on contact links as "intent", not as confirmed enquiries. Google Analytics loads when a page loads and sets its cookies immediately; this site does not show a consent banner, so there is no prompt to accept or reject it. To opt out, block analytics cookies or the googletagmanager.com domain in your browser settings or an extension, use a browser that blocks trackers by default, or install Google'sAnalytics opt-out add-on.
- Scheduling
  Calls are booked through Calendly. When you use the embedded calendar or booking link, Calendly's own privacy policy applies to the information you enter there.
- No accounts or portals
  This website is public marketing content. It does not offer a login, client portal or SSO endpoint, and it does not host private client data.
- AI crawlers
  Public pages may be read by search engines and AI assistants so that people can find accurate information about MV.tech. Machine-readable summaries are published at/llms.txtand/llms-full.txt.
- Contact
  Questions about this notice or about your data:contact@mvtech.solutions.
Responsible use

### Automation, data extraction and AI, done properly.

- Authorised access only. Integrations and data extraction use supported interfaces, honour source terms and rate limits, and are limited to client-approved use cases.
- Humans stay in control. Automated workflows keep review where judgment is required; AI assistants act only on approved data and tools, with permissions enforced in the application rather than in a prompt.
- Evaluated before expansion. AI features are tested against real questions and failure cases, including what happens when the answer is not in the source material, before their audience is widened.
- Your data stays yours. Client data is not used to train third-party models, and any use of AI tooling in delivery follows your policies.
Security or compliance questions?

### Ask before we start. We prefer it.

Procurement, security and legal questions are easiest to answer at the scoping stage. Bring your requirements and we will tell you plainly what we can and cannot commit to.

What happens next

### From first call to a written next step.

- 01 — We talk for 30 minutes — You describe the result you need, the current setup and your constraints. We ask the questions an engineer would ask and tell you honestly whether we are the right fit.
- 02 — You receive a written proposal — A first milestone with deliverables, acceptance criteria, assumptions, the overlap hours in your timezone and the price for that scope. Usually within a few business days.
- 03 — Work starts on your terms — Once the scope is agreed, we set up access, tools and the collaboration window, and begin delivering reviewable increments.
Three things to bring

### Make the first conversation count.

- The result you need. The workflow, report, application or AI feature, and what should be better when the work is done.
- The current setup. The systems involved, what already works and what keeps getting in the way. A description or a sanitised example is enough to start.
- Your working constraints. Timezone, preferred overlap, target date and any budget range. These shape a useful first scope.

# FAQ: Working with MV.tech, a Remote-First Consultancy Worldwide

URL: https://mvtech.solutions/faq/
Description: Answers about MV.tech: where we are based, timezone overlap with US, UK, EU and Australian clients, costs, services, credentials, security and how projects start.
Last modified: 2026-09-12

FAQ

## Remote consulting questions, answered plainly.

Everything people usually want to know before booking a call: who we are, where we are, how timezones and costs work, what we build and how we protect your data. If your question is not here, ask us directly.

The company

### Who MV.tech is.

**What is MV.tech?**
MV.tech is a remote-first technology consultancy based in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, India. We provide data engineering, custom software development, workflow automation, AI development (including RAG systems and MCP servers), IT staff augmentation and technology recruitment to clients worldwide. The company was founded by engineer Meet Vaghasia and is led by engineers rather than account managers.

**Is MV.tech the same as MV Tech Solutions or MVTech?**
Yes. MV.tech is the official brand and mvtech.solutions is the official website. People also search for it as MVTech, MV Tech, M V Tech, MV Tech Ahmedabad, MV Tech Solutions or MV Tech Data Solutions. They all refer to the same company.

**Where is MV.tech based, and where are your clients?**
We are based in Ahmedabad, India, and deliver fully remotely. Our clients are in India and worldwide, including North America, the United Kingdom, continental Europe, the Gulf and Asia-Pacific.

**How big is the team?**
Deliberately small. MV.tech is a focused team of senior specialists across data, software, cloud, automation and AI, led by founder Meet Vaghasia. We scale a specific engagement with additional specialists when the scope needs it, and say so when it does not.

**Has MV.tech worked with large companies?**
Our engineers have worked with organisations including Google, Volvo, BCW, RootstockLabs, Chainlabs, Toptal and Turing, directly or through vetted talent platforms. These names describe experience, not endorsements, current partnerships or sponsorships.

Timezones & cost

### Working with a team in India.

**Can a team in India overlap US, UK, European or Australian working hours?**
Yes. India Standard Time (UTC+5:30) overlaps the working day of every major business region for part of the day. Typical collaboration windows we plan around are 9:00 am to 1:00 pm US Eastern, 7:00 am to 10:00 am US Pacific, 9:00 am to 3:30 pm in the UK, 9:00 am to 4:00 pm in Central Europe, most of the business day in the Gulf, and 12:30 pm to 6:00 pm in eastern Australia. Exact hours are agreed per engagement.

**Does timezone overlap mean 24/7 support?**
No. Overlap means agreed working hours for collaboration: standups, reviews, demos and releases. Any support coverage, response-time expectations or release windows are defined separately in the engagement scope.

**How does MV.tech keep consulting costs lean?**
We operate as a focused remote team, so you pay for senior delivery time rather than offices, account-management layers, sales teams or idle bench capacity. Pricing is agreed per engagement against a written scope. We do not claim to be the cheapest option; we aim to be the best value for senior work with direct access to the people doing it.

**How are projects priced?**
Each engagement is priced against its written scope: deliverables, integrations, data volumes, testing, documentation and support. Embedded consultants are priced on agreed capacity and duration; recruitment fees are agreed per role. You receive the price before committing, and comparisons with other proposals should use the same scope and support expectations.

**How do you communicate between meetings?**
In your tools where possible: Slack or Teams, Jira or Linear, GitHub or GitLab, Google Workspace or Microsoft 365. Progress, decisions and open questions are written down so your stakeholders stay informed without another meeting.

Services & delivery

### What we build and how.

**What does MV.tech build?**
Data pipelines and cloud data platforms, dashboards and reporting layers, web applications and client portals, internal tools and business apps, workflow automations and API integrations, web scraping systems, RAG knowledge assistants, MCP servers and custom AI features integrated into existing products.

**Can you handle both the product interface and the data backend?**
Yes. The work can cover responsive front-end screens, API-backed workflows, data ingestion, warehouse modelling, analytics and deployment handover. The scope defines which parts your team owns and which parts we own.

**Do you support or improve existing systems?**
Yes. We can review and improve existing scripts, pipelines, APIs, dashboards, websites and applications while preserving current business workflows. A bounded review is often the most useful first engagement.

**How do projects usually start?**
With a 30-minute scoping call or an emailed brief. We clarify the goal, systems and constraints, then propose a first milestone with deliverables, acceptance criteria, review points and overlap hours. Work starts once that scope is agreed in writing.

**What is the difference between a project, staff augmentation and recruitment?**
In a project, MV.tech owns a defined scope and its deliverables. In staff augmentation, our consultants work inside your team under your technical leads for an agreed capacity. In recruitment, we help you hire a permanent employee into your own organisation. Each has its own scope and commercial terms.

Security & trust

### How we treat your data and systems.

**How do you handle access to our systems and data?**
With least-privilege access granted by you, separated development and production environments, and credentials stored in your secret management rather than shared in chat or documents. Access is reviewed during the engagement and removed at handover. Credentials are never needed for an initial enquiry.

**Will you sign an NDA or work under our contract?**
Yes. Mutual NDAs before detailed discussions are routine, and we can work under your master services agreement or provide a straightforward engagement agreement covering scope, ownership, confidentiality and payment terms.

**Who owns the deliverables?**
You do. Code, infrastructure definitions, documentation and data models are delivered into your repositories and accounts, with ownership stated in the engagement agreement.

**Do you use AI tools when building for clients?**
Where it helps and where your policy allows. AI-assisted development is reviewed by senior engineers like any other code, and client data is not used to train third-party models. Tell us your constraints and we work within them.

Still have a question?

### Ask the engineers directly.

Book a 30-minute call or email us. We respond to every enquiry, usually within one business day.

# 12 Questions to Ask Before Hiring a Data Consultancy | MV.tech

URL: https://mvtech.solutions/insights/questions-to-ask-before-hiring-a-remote-data-engineering-consultancy/
Description: A buyer's checklist for choosing a remote data engineering partner: who does the work, how the first milestone is scoped, how correctness is proven and what is included.
Last modified: 2026-09-10

Buyer's guide

## 12 Questions to Ask Before Hiring a Remote Data Engineering Consultancy

A buyer's checklist for choosing a remote data engineering partner: who does the work, how the first milestone is scoped, how correctness is proven and what is included.

By Meet Vaghasia, Founder & Lead Engineer · Published 10 September 2026 · 5 min read

In brief

- Most failed data projects fail on people and process, not technology. Ask who will actually write the code and how correctness will be proven.
- Good vendors propose a small first milestone with acceptance criteria. Vendors who quote the whole roadmap on day one are guessing.
- Compare proposals on the same scope, seniority, testing, documentation and support. A low headline price that excludes reconciliation and monitoring is not low.
Choosing a data engineering partner is difficult because the output is invisible until it is wrong. A pipeline can run green for months while quietly dropping records, and a dashboard can look finished while the numbers underneath it are unreliable. The questions below are the ones we would want a client to ask us, grouped by what they reveal. Use them as a checklist in your first conversations with any remote consultancy, including this one.

### People

#### 1. Who exactly will do the work, and can we meet them before we sign?

Why it matters: Proposals are often written by senior people and delivered by junior ones. A good answer: named engineers, their backgrounds, and a call with them before commitment. Be cautious if the main contact will be an account manager rather than an engineer.

#### 2. How senior is the person who will review the code and the data?

Why it matters: Data work is full of judgment calls about grain, deduplication, late-arriving records and business definitions. A good answer: a specific senior engineer accountable for review, with examples of the kind of issues they catch.

#### 3. What happens if that person is unavailable?

Why it matters: Continuity is the real difference between a consultancy and a freelancer. A good answer: documented systems, a second engineer familiar with the work, and a handover process, not just "we have a big team".

### Method

#### 4. What would you propose as the first milestone, and how would we know it worked?

Why it matters: A vendor who cannot narrow the problem cannot estimate it. A good answer: one dependable reporting flow, one source integrated end to end, or one bounded review, with written acceptance criteria such as "matches the finance ledger to within 0.1% for the last twelve months".

#### 5. How will you prove the numbers are right?

Why it matters: "The job succeeded" and "the data is correct" are different statements. A good answer: reconciliation against source records, checks for freshness and completeness, tests for edge cases such as empty periods and reprocessed records, and a plan for what happens when a check fails.

#### 6. What will operating this look like after you leave?

Why it matters: Pipelines are run far longer than they are built. A good answer: schedules and ownership documented, alerts that reach a human, recovery steps for common failures, and source-to-report mappings your own team can follow.

### Commercials

#### 7. What does the price include, and what does it exclude?

Why it matters: Testing, documentation, monitoring and handover are where cheap proposals save money. A good answer: an itemised scope that names these explicitly. Ask two vendors to price the same written scope and the comparison becomes meaningful.

#### 8. Who owns the code, the infrastructure and the data models?

Why it matters: Some vendors deliver into their own accounts and charge to release them. A good answer: everything in your repositories and cloud accounts from day one, with ownership stated in the agreement.

#### 9. How do you handle changes in scope?

Why it matters: Requirements will change once real data appears. A good answer: changes are written down, estimated and agreed before they are built, and assumptions that prove wrong are raised immediately rather than absorbed silently or invoiced later.

### Working model

#### 10. Which hours will you overlap with us, in our local time?

Why it matters: "We adapt to your timezone" is not a commitment. A good answer: a specific recurring window, the meetings that live inside it, and how progress is communicated outside it. See our timezone playbook for what realistic windows look like.

#### 11. Where will decisions and progress be recorded?

Why it matters: Remote work fails when decisions live in someone's memory. A good answer: your tools, your wiki, your ticketing system; written standups and decision records you could forward to a stakeholder without editing.

### Evidence

#### 12. What can you show us, and what can you not?

Why it matters: Confidentiality limits what any consultancy can share, but it does not eliminate evidence. A good answer: verified credentials with links, anonymised descriptions of comparable work, a sample scope document or runbook, and honesty about what is under NDA. Be wary of logos without context and of testimonials that cannot be attributed.

### How to run the comparison

- Write one page describing the outcome you need, the systems involved, approximate data volumes and your working hours.
- Send the same page to each shortlisted vendor and ask for a first-milestone proposal, not a roadmap.
- Score the proposals on the twelve questions above before you look at the price.
- Only then compare prices, adjusting for what each proposal excludes.
Vendors who respond to a one-page brief with specific questions of their own are usually the ones who will find the problems in your data before your finance team does.

### Frequently asked questions

**Should we start with a data audit or go straight to building?**
If you already have pipelines and reports that people distrust, a short bounded review is usually the best first engagement: it produces a prioritised list of what is actually broken. If you are starting from spreadsheets and exports, build one dependable reporting flow end to end; it teaches both sides more than an audit would.

**Is a remote consultancy in India a reasonable choice for a US or UK company?**
Yes, provided the overlap hours, communication practices and accountability are explicit. The structural cost advantage is real because you are not paying for offices and account layers, but it only helps if the seniority and the working model are right. Apply the same twelve questions you would apply to a local firm.

**What should we share before the first call?**
The report or workflow you want to improve, the source systems, rough data volumes, the tools you use today and the refresh frequency you need. A description or a sanitised example is enough; credentials are never needed for an enquiry.

# RAG vs Fine-Tuning for Internal Knowledge Assistants | MV.tech

URL: https://mvtech.solutions/insights/rag-vs-fine-tuning-for-internal-knowledge-assistants/
Description: A plain-language comparison of retrieval-augmented generation and fine-tuning for company knowledge assistants: when each fits, permissions, evaluation and cost.
Last modified: 2026-09-10

AI engineering

## RAG vs Fine-Tuning: Choosing the Right Approach for an Internal Knowledge Assistant

A plain-language comparison of retrieval-augmented generation and fine-tuning for company knowledge assistants: when each fits, permissions, evaluation and cost.

By Meet Vaghasia, Founder & Lead Engineer · Published 10 September 2026 · 5 min read

In brief

- Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) gives a language model the relevant passages from your own documents at question time. Fine-tuning changes the model's weights using examples, which teaches behaviour and style far better than it teaches facts.
- For assistants that answer questions about company knowledge, RAG is almost always the right starting point: it stays current, can cite sources and can respect user permissions. Fine-tuning suits narrow, repetitive tasks with a stable format.
- Whichever you choose, the deciding work is retrieval quality, access control and evaluation against real questions, including the ones the documents cannot answer.
Teams that want an assistant over their own documents, tickets and data usually ask the same first question: should we fine-tune a model on our content, or use retrieval? The short answer is that these techniques solve different problems, and for internal knowledge the answer is usually retrieval first, with fine-tuning added later only if a specific, measurable need appears. Here is the reasoning, without the jargon.

### What each approach actually does

#### Retrieval-augmented generation

RAG splits your documents into passages, indexes them (typically with embeddings and often a keyword index as well), and at question time retrieves the passages most relevant to the question. Those passages are placed in the model's context along with the question, and the model writes an answer grounded in them. The model itself is unchanged; what changes is what it is shown.

#### Fine-tuning

Fine-tuning continues training a model on examples of inputs and desired outputs, adjusting its weights. It is effective at teaching a model how to behave: a tone of voice, a strict output format, a domain's vocabulary, or a narrow classification task. It is a poor way to store facts that change, because updating a fact means retraining, and a fine-tuned model still cannot tell you which document its answer came from.

### A side-by-side comparison

RAG and fine-tuning compared for company knowledge assistants
| Consideration | Retrieval-augmented generation | Fine-tuning |
| Keeping up with changing content | Re-index the changed documents; answers update immediately | Retrain and redeploy; facts baked into weights go stale |
| Citing sources | Natural: the answer can link to the passages it used | Not available; the model cannot show where an answer came from |
| Respecting user permissions | Filter retrieval by what the current user may see | Everything in the training data is available to every user |
| Handling questions outside the material | Can detect weak retrieval and say "I don't know" | Tends to answer confidently anyway |
| Teaching format, tone or a narrow task | Possible through prompting, with limits | Strong: this is what fine-tuning is for |
| Upfront cost | Engineering time for ingestion, retrieval and evaluation | Curating thousands of quality examples plus training runs |
| Ongoing cost | Longer prompts per query; index maintenance | Hosting or serving a custom model; periodic retraining |

### When RAG is the right choice

- The assistant must answer from documents, policies, tickets or records that change over time.
- Users need to see where an answer came from before they trust it.
- Different users are allowed to see different things, so permissions must be enforced at retrieval time.
- The content is too large or too varied to summarise into training examples.
This describes almost every internal knowledge assistant we are asked to build: HR and policy questions, engineering runbooks, customer-support knowledge, contract and procedure lookups.

### When fine-tuning earns its place

- A narrow, repetitive task with a stable format: classifying tickets, extracting fields from a known document type, writing in a strict house style.
- Prompting has been tried and measured, and the remaining error rate is about behaviour rather than missing information.
- Latency or cost per request matters enough that a smaller, specialised model is worth the maintenance.
Fine-tuning and RAG are not mutually exclusive. A common mature design uses retrieval for knowledge and a lightly fine-tuned or carefully prompted model for consistent behaviour. Start with retrieval and good prompting; add fine-tuning when you can name the metric it will improve.

### The work that actually decides success

#### Retrieval quality

Most "the AI is wrong" complaints are retrieval failures: the right passage was never shown to the model. Chunking that respects document structure, combining semantic and keyword search, adding metadata filters and re-ranking results all matter more than the choice of model. Measure retrieval separately from answer quality so you can tell which one is failing.

#### Access control

Permissions must be enforced in the application before retrieval, using the user's identity and the source system's rules. Instructions written into a prompt are not access control; a determined user can talk a model out of them. This is a design requirement, not a feature to add later.

#### Evaluation with real questions

Collect the questions people actually ask, including ones the documents cannot answer, and review the assistant's behaviour on them before widening the audience. Score groundedness (is the answer supported by the retrieved passages?), correctness, and how the assistant behaves when it should decline. Keep the set and re-run it after every change to the index, prompt or model.

#### Unanswerable questions

A good assistant says "I could not find this in the approved sources" and points to a human. A bad one improvises. Build the decline path deliberately, test it, and make it easy for users to report wrong answers.

### A sensible first project

Choose one defined collection of documents and a small group of users. Collect twenty to fifty real questions. Build retrieval and answering over that collection, with source references and a decline path, and review the results with the users. Only then decide on wider access, automated actions or any fine-tuning. This bounded first release typically takes weeks rather than months, and it produces the evidence you need to justify the next step.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does fine-tuning make a model "know" our documents?**
Not reliably. Fine-tuning shapes how a model responds far more than what it can recall, and it cannot cite where an answer came from. If the goal is accurate answers about specific documents, retrieval is the mechanism that puts the right text in front of the model.

**Will our data be used to train someone else's model?**
It depends on the provider and the contract terms you select. Business and API tiers of the major model providers generally state that customer data is not used for training, but this should be confirmed in writing and reflected in your architecture, including where indexes and logs are stored.

**How much does an internal knowledge assistant cost to run?**
Ongoing costs come from model usage per query, the retrieval infrastructure, and keeping the index current as documents change. For most internal tools these are modest compared with the engineering time to build and evaluate the system properly. Ask for both numbers when comparing proposals.

About the author

# Staff Augmentation vs Project Consulting vs Recruitment | MV.tech

URL: https://mvtech.solutions/insights/staff-augmentation-vs-project-consulting-vs-recruitment/
Description: How to choose between embedding a consultant, commissioning a scoped project and hiring permanently for data, software and AI work: control, cost, speed and risk.
Last modified: 2026-09-10

Engagement models

## Staff Augmentation vs Project Consulting vs Recruitment: Which Engagement Model Fits?

How to choose between embedding a consultant, commissioning a scoped project and hiring permanently for data, software and AI work: control, cost, speed and risk.

By Meet Vaghasia, Founder & Lead Engineer · Published 10 September 2026 · 5 min read

In brief

- Choose ascoped projectwhen the outcome is clear and you want someone else accountable for delivering it.
- Choosestaff augmentationwhen the work is ongoing or still taking shape and you want senior capacity working under your own direction.
- Choosepermanent recruitmentwhen the role will exist for years and belongs inside your organisation.
- Many teams combine them: a project to prove the approach, an embedded consultant to extend it, a permanent hire once the role is understood.
When a company needs more data, software or AI capability than it has, there are three ways to get it: commission a project, bring outside people into the team, or hire. They are often confused, sometimes deliberately by vendors who sell whichever they have available. This guide separates them by the questions that actually matter: who directs the work, who carries the risk, how quickly it starts and what it costs over time.

### The three models, defined

#### Scoped project consulting

You describe an outcome; the consultancy proposes a scope with deliverables, milestones and acceptance criteria, then delivers it. The consultancy directs its own people and is accountable for the result. Typical examples: a first data pipeline and reporting layer, an internal application, an automation of a specific process, a knowledge assistant over a defined document set.

#### Staff augmentation (embedded consultants or a dedicated team)

Senior specialists join your team for an agreed capacity and duration, working in your tools, your rituals and your hours, under the direction of your technical leads. You own the backlog and the priorities; the consultancy supplies the people, the continuity and the quality bar. Typical examples: a data engineer alongside your product team for two quarters, an AI engineer to build out an assistant your team has designed, additional senior developers during a delivery crunch.

#### Technology recruitment

You hire a permanent employee into your organisation. A recruitment partner helps define the role, find and assess candidates and coordinate the process; you make the hiring decision and employ the person directly. Typical examples: a head of data, a lead engineer for a new product, a permanent platform team.

### Side by side

Engagement models compared
| Question | Scoped project | Staff augmentation | Permanent recruitment |
| Who directs the day-to-day work? | The consultancy, against an agreed scope | Your technical leads | You, as the employer |
| Who carries delivery risk? | Shared, with the consultancy accountable for the scope | Mostly you; the consultancy is accountable for the person's quality and continuity | You |
| How quickly does it start? | After scoping, typically one to three weeks | Usually fastest once a fit is confirmed | Slowest: weeks to months depending on the role |
| Best when | The outcome is clear and bounded | The work is ongoing or still emerging | The role is long-term and core to the business |
| Cost structure | Fixed or milestone-based price for the scope | Agreed capacity and duration, priced accordingly | A recruitment fee plus ongoing salary and overheads |
| Knowledge stays with | You, via documentation and handover | Your team, because the work happens inside it | You, as long as the employee stays |
| Flexibility to stop or change | At milestone boundaries | High, within the notice terms | Low; hiring is a long-term commitment |

### How to decide

#### Start from the shape of the work

If you can write the outcome on one page with acceptance criteria, it is a project. If you can only describe a stream of work and a direction, it is capacity, which points to augmentation. If you can describe a role that will still exist in three years, it is a hire.

#### Then consider who should be in control

Project consulting suits teams that want to buy an outcome and get on with their own work. Augmentation suits teams with strong technical leadership who want more senior hands without giving up direction. Recruitment suits organisations building durable in-house capability.

#### Then think about risk and reversibility

A project has a natural end and clear acceptance, which limits the downside. Augmentation is easy to scale up or down. A permanent hire is the largest commitment and the hardest to reverse, which is why it deserves the most careful brief.

### Common mistakes

- Buying a project when you need a team.Fixed scopes fight with emerging requirements. If the roadmap is uncertain, embed people instead.
- Buying "staff augmentation" that is really outsourcing.If you never meet the engineers and cannot direct them, it is not augmentation, whatever the contract says.
- Hiring permanently for a temporary spike.Six months of intense delivery followed by maintenance is a job for consultants, not a new headcount line.
- Treating recruitment and consulting as interchangeable.They have different scopes, fees and obligations. A good partner will tell you which one you are actually asking for.

### Combining the models

The most effective sequence we see is: a scoped project to prove an approach and establish trust; an embedded consultant to extend it while priorities settle; and a permanent hire once the organisation understands the role well enough to write it. Each step reduces the risk of the next. A partner that offers all three, as MV.tech does, can move with you through that sequence without a change of vendor, but the model you choose at each step should follow the work, not the vendor's preference.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is staff augmentation the same as outsourcing?**
No. In staff augmentation, named consultants work inside your team under your direction, in your tools and your hours. In outsourcing, a vendor takes over a function or a scope and directs its own people. Augmentation keeps control and knowledge with you; outsourcing trades some of that for a managed outcome.

**Can an embedded consultant work in our timezone?**
Yes, within an agreed window. A remote consultant in India can typically overlap US Eastern mornings, most of the UK and European working day, Gulf business hours or Australian afternoons. The specific hours, meetings and response expectations should be written into the engagement.

**Can a consultant later become a permanent hire?**
Sometimes, if all parties agree and the arrangement allows it. It is better to decide up front whether the engagement is intended as a trial for a permanent role and to set the terms accordingly than to negotiate it under pressure later.

He is a senior data and AI engineer who builds ETL pipelines and cloud warehouses on BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift and PostgreSQL, semantic and reporting layers for Power BI, Tableau and Looker Studio, and AI automation using RAG, MCP servers and custom AI connectors. # Working With an India Engineering Team Across Timezones | MV.tech

URL: https://mvtech.solutions/insights/timezone-overlap-with-an-india-based-engineering-team/
Description: Realistic overlap windows, what to agree before you start and the async habits that make a remote engineering team in India work for US, UK, EU and Australian companies.
Last modified: 2026-09-10

Remote delivery playbook

## How to Work with an India-Based Engineering Team Across Timezones

Realistic overlap windows, what to agree before you start and the async habits that make a remote engineering team in India work for US, UK, EU and Australian companies.

By Meet Vaghasia, Founder & Lead Engineer · Published 10 September 2026 · 6 min read

In brief

- India Standard Time (UTC+5:30) overlaps the working day of every major business region for part of the day, so the question is never "is overlap possible?" but "which hours, and what happens outside them?"
- Agree four things before work starts: the collaboration window, where decisions get recorded, response expectations, and release windows. Most timezone problems are really unwritten-expectation problems.
- Treat "24/7 coverage" claims and unnamed engineers as warning signs. Ask for the specific hours and the specific people.
Companies hesitate about remote teams in India for one reason more than any other: the clock. The worry is reasonable, and it is also solvable, because it is mostly a planning problem rather than a geography problem. This guide covers what realistic overlap looks like from different regions, what to agree before an engagement begins, and the working habits that make distributed delivery feel closer than it is.

### Where India sits on the clock

India Standard Time is UTC+5:30 all year; India does not observe daylight saving. That places an Indian working day roughly like this relative to other regions:

- United Kingdom and Europe:India is 4.5 to 5.5 hours ahead of London and 3.5 to 4.5 hours ahead of Berlin, depending on the season. An engineer working a standard Indian day shares most of the UK and European morning and early afternoon.
- North America:India is 9.5 to 10.5 hours ahead of US Eastern time and 12.5 to 13.5 hours ahead of Pacific. A standard Indian day barely touches the US morning, so teams that serve American clients shift their hours later, typically starting around midday IST, to cover the US morning.
- Gulf:India is only 1.5 hours ahead of Dubai. Overlap is almost the whole day.
- Asia-Pacific:India is 2.5 hours behind Singapore and 4.5 to 5.5 hours behind Sydney, so Australian afternoons coincide with Indian mornings.
The practical conclusion: a team in India can give a European client a half-day of overlap without any adjustment, and can give an American client three to four hours every morning by shifting its day. It cannot give a single client both a full US afternoon and a full Australian morning with the same people, and any vendor who implies otherwise is describing something other than a normal working week.

### Typical overlap windows

These are the windows we plan engagements around at MV.tech. Yours may differ; the point is that they are specific.

Illustrative collaboration windows for a team in Ahmedabad, India
| Your team | Overlap in your local time | Equivalent in IST |
| New York (US Eastern) | 9:00 am – 1:00 pm | 6:30 pm – 10:30 pm |
| San Francisco (US Pacific) | 7:00 am – 10:00 am | 7:30 pm – 10:30 pm |
| London | 9:00 am – 3:30 pm | 1:30 pm – 8:00 pm |
| Berlin (Central Europe) | 9:00 am – 4:00 pm | 12:30 pm – 7:30 pm |
| Dubai (Gulf) | 9:00 am – 6:00 pm | 10:30 am – 7:30 pm |
| Singapore | 11:00 am – 6:00 pm | 8:30 am – 3:30 pm |
| Sydney (Australia East) | 12:30 pm – 6:00 pm | 8:00 am – 1:30 pm |
Two things are worth noticing. First, the windows are three to seven hours long, which is enough for standups, reviews, pairing and releases; nobody needs eight hours of shared screen time to deliver software well. Second, the windows shift by an hour when your region changes its clocks, so write the window in your local time and let the vendor adjust.

### Four things to agree before the first sprint

#### 1. The collaboration window, in your time

Write down the recurring hours during which the team is reachable synchronously, which meetings live inside them, and who attends. "Flexible" is not a window. "9:00 am to 1:00 pm Eastern, Monday to Friday, with standup at 9:15" is.

#### 2. Where decisions live

Distributed teams fail when decisions are made in a call and then forgotten by the half of the team that was asleep. Choose one place, such as a decision log in your wiki, pull request descriptions or a pinned channel, and make "write it down where the other side will see it" a habit, not a favour.

#### 3. Response expectations outside the window

Say explicitly what "urgent" means, how it is raised, and what response is expected outside the window. Most engagements need no out-of-hours coverage at all; production systems that do need it should have it written into the scope with named responsibilities, not implied by a sales conversation.

#### 4. Release windows

Decide when changes may reach production and who must be awake when they do. A team that deploys during the client's morning, with the client's own engineers online, avoids most of the drama associated with remote delivery.

### Async habits that actually work

- Written standups.Three lines per person, posted before the client's day begins: done, next, blocked. Ten minutes of reading replaces a meeting nobody wanted at 7:00 am.
- Recorded demos.A five-minute screen recording of a working feature, shared in the channel, lets stakeholders review at their convenience and reply with timestamps.
- Pull requests that explain themselves.What changed, why, how it was tested, what to look at first. Reviews then happen across the time gap instead of waiting for a call.
- Handover notes at the end of each day.Where things stand, what was decided, what needs an answer. The other side starts its morning informed rather than guessing.
- One synchronous ritual that never moves.A weekly review inside the window, with a demo and a look at the plan. Everything else can flex; this cannot.

### What should still be synchronous

Discovery conversations, design decisions with real trade-offs, incident response, and anything involving disagreement. If a thread has gone back and forth three times without converging, book fifteen minutes inside the window and settle it. Async is a default, not a religion.

### Warning signs when evaluating a remote vendor

- "We provide 24/7 support"from a team of five. Ask who exactly is awake at 3:00 am your time and what they are authorised to do.
- No named engineersbefore signing. If you cannot meet the people who will do the work, you are buying a promise, not a team.
- A dedicated account manageras the main contact. Useful in a large programme, but for a small engagement it usually means the engineers are somewhere behind a wall.
- Vague overlap."We adjust to your timezone" without hours attached is a sentence, not a commitment.

### The cost dimension, briefly

The economic case for a remote team in India is real, but it is often described badly. The saving does not come from cheap labour; senior engineers in India are not cheap, nor should they be. It comes from what you are not paying for: offices in expensive cities, account-management layers, idle bench capacity and brand premiums. A lean remote consultancy passes that structural difference through. Compare proposals on the same scope, the same seniority and the same support expectations, and the difference is still substantial without being suspicious.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does India observe daylight saving time?**
No. India Standard Time stays at UTC+5:30 all year. Overlap windows written in a client's local time shift by an hour in IST when the client's region changes its clocks, which is why the window should be defined in the client's time.

**Can a team in India cover US Pacific hours?**
Yes, for part of the day. A common arrangement is 7:00 am to 10:00 am Pacific, which is 7:30 pm to 10:30 pm in India. Some teams run a later shift to cover more of the Pacific morning; a full Pacific afternoon is unrealistic for a team keeping a normal week.

**How much overlap does a software project really need?**
In our experience, three to four hours of daily overlap is enough for standups, reviews, pairing on hard problems and releases, provided decisions and progress are written down. More overlap is pleasant; it is rarely what determines whether a project succeeds.

# What Is an MCP Server, and When Should a Business Build One? | MV.tech

URL: https://mvtech.solutions/insights/what-is-an-mcp-server-and-when-should-a-business-build-one/
Description: A business-level explanation of the Model Context Protocol: what an MCP server exposes, when building one makes sense, the security decisions involved and a first project.
Last modified: 2026-09-10

AI engineering

## What Is an MCP Server, and When Should a Business Build One?

A business-level explanation of the Model Context Protocol: what an MCP server exposes, when building one makes sense, the security decisions involved and a first project.

By Meet Vaghasia, Founder & Lead Engineer · Published 10 September 2026 · 5 min read

In brief

- The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that lets AI applications connect to external tools and data through one consistent interface. An MCP server is the piece you build around your systems so that compatible AI assistants can use them.
- Build one when several AI clients need the same governed access to internal systems, when off-the-shelf connectors do not exist for your tools, or when you need authorisation and logging in one place rather than in every prompt.
- Treat an MCP server as production software: authentication, least-privilege tool design, human approval for consequential actions and audit logs are part of the scope, not extras.
Every business that tries to make an AI assistant useful eventually hits the same wall: the assistant needs to look things up in, or act on, systems the model has never seen. Customer records, ticket queues, order status, internal documentation, the finance system. The Model Context Protocol is the emerging standard way to make those connections, and "MCP server development" has become a common request from teams who want their AI tools to do more than chat. This guide explains what an MCP server is in practical terms, when it is worth building one, and what to insist on if you do.

### What MCP is

MCP is an open protocol, originally released by Anthropic in late 2024 and since supported across the major AI assistant and developer platforms, that standardises how an AI application (the client) discovers and uses capabilities offered by an external program (the server). The full specification and reference implementations are published at modelcontextprotocol.io.

Before MCP, connecting an assistant to a system meant writing a custom integration for each combination of assistant and system. With MCP, a system exposes its capabilities once, and any compatible client, whether a chat assistant, a coding tool or an internal agent, can use them the same way.

### What an MCP server exposes

- Tools:actions the assistant can call, with typed inputs and outputs. For examplelookup_order(order_id),create_ticket(summary, priority)orrun_approved_report(name, date_range).
- Resources:data the assistant can read, such as a document, a record or a query result, identified by a URI.
- Prompts:reusable, parameterised instructions that package a well-tested way of doing a task, for example "prepare a weekly status summary from these sources".
The server describes these capabilities in a machine-readable way, the client shows them to the model, and the model decides when to use them. The server, not the model, enforces what is allowed.

### When building an MCP server makes sense

- Your systems have no ready-made connector.Internal databases, custom applications, older business systems and in-house APIs rarely come with an MCP integration. Building one is how they join the conversation.
- Several AI clients need the same access.If your support assistant, your internal chat tool and a coding agent all need to read the same records, one server with consistent rules beats three bespoke integrations.
- Governance has to live in one place.An MCP server is where you enforce who may do what, log every call and shape which data leaves the system. That is far more reliable than instructions inside prompts.
- You want the assistant to act, not just answer.Creating tickets, updating records, triggering workflows: actions need typed inputs, validation and often human approval, which is exactly what a tool interface provides.

### When you probably do not need one

- One application, one model, one integration that will never be reused. A direct API call inside that application is simpler.
- The system you want to connect already has a well-maintained MCP server from its vendor. Evaluate it before building.
- The real problem is that the assistant cannot answer from documents. That is a retrieval problem; seeRAG versus fine-tuning. MCP can expose a retrieval tool, but the retrieval quality is the work.

### Security decisions you cannot skip

#### Authentication and identity

The server must know who is asking. Remote servers should use standards-based authentication, such as OAuth, and pass the user's identity through to the underlying systems so that existing permissions apply. A server that connects with one privileged service account on behalf of everyone is a data leak waiting for a clever prompt.

#### Least-privilege tool design

Expose narrow, purpose-built tools rather than "run any query" or "call any endpoint". Validate inputs, cap result sizes and separate read tools from write tools. The model will use whatever it is given; the server decides what that is.

#### Human approval for consequential actions

Anything that spends money, changes customer-facing records or sends communications should require an explicit confirmation step, either in the client's interface or in the workflow the tool triggers. Design the approval path into the tool, not around it.

#### Logging and audit

Record every tool call with the caller, the arguments and the outcome. This is how you debug odd behaviour, satisfy security reviews and answer the question "why did the assistant do that?"

#### Untrusted content

Data returned by a tool may contain text that tries to instruct the model (a classic prompt injection). Servers should treat returned content as data, clients should display it as such, and consequential actions should never be triggered by content alone.

### What a sensible first MCP project looks like

- Pick one system and two or three toolsthat would remove real friction, for example looking up a customer, summarising their recent tickets and drafting (not sending) a reply.
- Define the tool contractswith typed inputs, outputs, error cases and result limits, and agree which are read-only.
- Wire authenticationso the user's own permissions apply, and add logging from the first commit.
- Test with the intended clientsand with real tasks, including attempts to misuse the tools, before widening access.
- Document ownership and operation: who maintains the server, how it is deployed, how tools are added and reviewed.
A project of this shape is typically weeks of work, and it produces something you can extend tool by tool as trust grows.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is MCP tied to one AI vendor?**
No. MCP is an open specification with open-source SDKs in several languages, and it is supported by multiple AI assistants, developer tools and platforms. A server you build can be used by any compatible client, which is the main reason to prefer it over a bespoke integration.

**Does an MCP server need to be hosted on the internet?**
Not necessarily. Servers can run locally alongside a desktop client using standard input and output, or remotely over HTTP for shared use. Remote servers need proper authentication and network controls; local servers still need careful tool design because they run with the user's own access.

**What does MCP server development cost?**
The main cost drivers are the number and complexity of tools, the authentication model, the systems being integrated, testing and documentation. A focused first server with a handful of well-designed tools is a small project; the cost grows with the sensitivity of the actions it enables and the rigour those actions demand.

# Our Delivery Process: Scoping Call to Production Handover | MV.tech

URL: https://mvtech.solutions/process/
Description: How MV.tech delivers remote engineering projects: a 30-minute scoping call, a written first milestone, reviewable increments in your timezone and a documented handover.
Last modified: 2026-09-11

How we work

## A clear remote delivery process from idea to production.

Execution first, without burying the project in ceremony. Every engagement follows the same five steps, whether we own a scoped project or work embedded in your team. You always know what is being built, who is doing it, and what happens next.

The engagement

### Five steps from first call to handover.

- 01 — Understand the goal — A 30-minute call to clarify what you are building, who it is for, the systems involved and what success looks like. We tell you honestly whether we are the right fit.
- 02 — Scope the first milestone — A written proposal with deliverables, acceptance criteria, assumptions, review points and the overlap hours in your timezone. Nothing starts until this is agreed.
- 03 — Build in reviewable increments — Working software, pipelines or automations you can see early and often. Decisions are recorded in your tools so stakeholders stay informed between calls.
- 04 — Test against reality — Reconcile outputs with source records, test failure paths and retries, check performance and access control before anything is called done.
- 05 — Deploy and hand over — Go live with documentation, monitoring and a clear support or handover plan. Then we agree the next useful increment, or you run it yourself.
What you receive

### Artefacts, not just activity.

- Scope document with milestones, acceptance criteria and explicit assumptions before work begins.
- Working demonstrations at each review point, in your collaboration window, with decisions written down afterwards.
- Source code and infrastructure in your repositories and accounts, with credentials and access under your control.
- Operating documentation: schedules, ownership, recovery steps, source mappings and known limitations.
- Monitoring and alerts so a job that "succeeded" with bad data does not go unnoticed.
- A support option sized to the system: ad-hoc, a monthly retainer or continued embedded capacity.
Working across timezones

### Overlap when it matters, async when it does not.

Discovery, demos, reviews and releases happen inside an agreed window in your local time. Between those, work continues in India Standard Time and you receive written updates you can forward without translation. Response expectations, release windows and any support coverage are written into the scope rather than assumed.

Process questions

### Frequently asked about how we deliver.

**How long does the first milestone usually take?**
Most first milestones are sized to deliver something working within a few weeks: one dependable reporting flow, one automated hand-off, one complete user journey or one bounded knowledge assistant. The exact duration is part of the written scope.

**Who owns the code and infrastructure?**
You do. Work is delivered into your repositories, cloud accounts and tools wherever possible, and ownership and licensing terms are stated in the engagement agreement.

**How do you handle changes in scope?**
New requirements are welcome; they are written down, estimated and either added to the current milestone by agreement or planned into the next one. Assumptions that turn out to be wrong are raised as soon as they are found.

**What happens after the handover?**
You can run the system yourself with the documentation provided, keep us on for ad-hoc support or a monthly retainer, or continue with embedded capacity. The support arrangement is agreed separately from the build.

Step one

### Start with the 30-minute scoping call.

Bring the goal, the systems involved and your preferred working hours. You leave with a written next step, whether or not that involves us.

### Practical AI consulting services

01

#### RAG and knowledge search

Plan document ingestion, chunking, retrieval and source references around a defined knowledge collection. Account for updates, permissions and questions the available material cannot answer, and put retrieval behind your own access rules.

02

#### AI automation and agentic workflows

Connect an assistant to a support workflow, internal tool or customer application. Multi-step workflows can retrieve context, generate SQL, validate a result and produce a formatted output, with permitted actions defined and a person in control of approvals and exceptions.

03

Build Model Context Protocol servers in Python that expose approved tools and data to compatible AI applications. Define tool inputs, resource access, authorisation through OAuth and managed secrets, and logging around the business systems being connected.

04

Connect enterprise AI platforms and agents to databases, APIs and internal tools with scoped, token-aware access. Package recurring tasks — retrieval, SQL generation, validation, formatted export — as reusable connectors, plugins and AI skills rather than one-off prompts.

#### Custom AI solutions

Integrate document processing, classification, extraction or decision support into an existing workflow. LLM-assisted extraction can pull structured records out of documents, APIs and web sources; agree the expected output, validation rules and review path before automating a business action.

Bring responses from GPT, Claude, Llama or Qwen into existing business logic and user interfaces. Validate inputs and outputs, handle failures, compare models against your own task, and keep application permissions under server-side control.

Agree representative questions and expected behaviour. Review source grounding, unsupported answers, latency and usage cost before expanding the feature's audience. Where an assistant touches financial or audited systems, access is scoped with OAuth and managed secrets and every tool call is logged, which is the kind of evidence a SOC 2 programme asks for.

Before we begin

### Questions about AI automation, RAG & MCP development.

Not answered here? Ask us directly or read the full FAQ.

**What is retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG?**
RAG retrieves relevant material from an approved source collection and provides it to a language model when generating an answer. It can help an assistant answer questions about your own information, but retrieval quality, access controls and evaluation still matter.

**What is MCP development?**
Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a shared interface for AI applications to connect to tools and data. We build MCP servers in Python around your approved APIs or systems, define the tools and resources they expose, handle authorisation with OAuth and managed secrets, and test them with the intended compatible clients. Access permissions and approval requirements remain part of the application design.

**Can an AI agent query our databases safely?**
It can, when access is engineered rather than prompted. In practice that means a connector or MCP server that authenticates as a scoped service identity, exposes only approved tables or endpoints, generates SQL against a governed reporting layer, validates the query and the result before returning it, and logs every call. Whitelists and read-only access keep an agent away from anything it has no business touching.

**Do we need to train our own AI model?**
Not necessarily. The right scope may use an existing model with retrieval and application integration. We review your use case, data, evaluation criteria and operating constraints before proposing an approach.

**Can the assistant respect different user permissions?**
Role-aware access can be part of the scope. The design must enforce authorisation before protected data is retrieved or an action is performed; instructions written into a prompt are not a substitute for application access controls.

**What determines the cost of an AI assistant?**
The main factors are source preparation, integrations, permission rules, evaluation, user interface and support. Ongoing costs also depend on model usage, retrieval infrastructure and traffic. These should be considered alongside the build estimate.

# Blockchain & On-Chain Data Analytics | MV.tech

URL: https://mvtech.solutions/services/blockchain-data-analytics/
Description: On-chain data engineering: decoded transactions and events, cross-chain ETL into BigQuery, token valuation, categorisation and reward reconciliation.
Last modified: 2026-09-12

Service · Remote-first senior specialists

## Blockchain & On-Chain Data Analytics

Raw chain data is not analytics. MV.tech decodes transactions, logs and events using contract ABIs and Web3.py, consolidates them across networks into BigQuery, and adds the valuation, categorisation and reconciliation layers that let finance, product and compliance teams answer questions about on-chain activity.

- Remote from Ahmedabad, India
- Overlap with your timezone
- Senior specialists, direct access
- Scope agreed in writing
The starting point

### When on-chain activity has to answer business questions

- A block explorer can show one transaction, but nobody can total a quarter across chains.
- Each network has its own ingestion script and its own idea of what a transaction record looks like.
- Finance needs token movements valued in fiat at the right timestamp, with fees attributed.
- Staking rewards are reconciled by hand and the totals never quite agree.
- A compliance or AML question needs wallet-level history and there is no dataset to query.
- Someone corrected a figure directly in the analytics table and the original value is gone.
- Token coverage is partial, so a material share of transfers lands in an "unknown" bucket.
What we deliver

### On-chain data engineering services

01

#### Cross-chain ingestion and ETL

Pull blocks, transactions, logs and events from node RPCs, indexers and chain APIs into a common schema in BigQuery. Reorg handling, backfills, checkpointing and per-chain rate limits are part of the pipeline rather than an afterthought. Work has covered Ethereum, Bitcoin, Immutable X, Immutable zkEVM, XDC, WEMIX, Tezos and Cardano.

02

#### Decoding transactions, logs and events

Apply contract ABIs with Web3.py to turn opaque input data and topics into named events with typed arguments: transfers, mints, burns, stakes, swaps. That includes proxy contracts, non-standard implementations and the contracts whose interface has to be reconstructed before anything can be read.

03

#### Token identification and valuation

Maintain token registries and price reference data, and value movements at the relevant block timestamp in the reporting currency, handling decimals, fee proration and FX explicitly. Widening mapping coverage is ordinary, high-value work: on past engagements it moved from 35 tokens to 42 and beyond, pulling material volume out of the unknown bucket.

04

#### Transaction categorisation

Classify activity into the categories the business reports on — transfer, trade, fee, reward, bridge, internal movement — using contract, method, counterparty and pattern rules that are written down and reviewable rather than buried inside a query.

05

#### Staking-reward reconciliation

Reward ledgers per validator, delegator or wallet, reconciled against on-chain distributions and internal records, with period totals, accrual timing and a discrepancy report. On past engagements a ledger of this kind has removed more than 70% of a manual reconciliation cycle.

06

#### Wallet analytics and attribution

Wallet-level histories, balances over time, cohort and retention views, and attribution of addresses to known entities or internal accounts, with the labelling maintained as data rather than hardcoded into reports.

07

#### Compliance and AML investigative datasets

Queryable datasets for investigation and monitoring: counterparty exposure, flows through addresses of interest, thresholds and time-windowed aggregates. They support an analyst’s judgement and an auditor’s questions; they do not replace either.

08

#### Immutable base data with an audit trail

Base tables hold exactly what the chain reported and are never edited. Manual corrections, whitelists and overrides live in separate layers applied when the reporting view is built, each carrying an author, a timestamp and a reason, so a figure can still be explained months later.

One chain done properly establishes the schema, the decoding patterns, the override model and the validation checks, so the second and third networks are mostly configuration rather than new engineering.
